name: Koasati
confidence_why: Kimball's grammar (1991) and dictionary (1994) describe a right-edge pitch accent on nouns (penult if it has a long vowel, otherwise the final syllable), while the instrumental studies of Gordon, Martin and Langley (2015) and Gordon and Martin (2023) find the first syllable most prominent, treat the final high pitch as phrase-level intonation, call Kimball's accent system "quite different from what we hear" and label their own stress analysis tentative, so two authoritative first-hand descriptions disagree on both placement and type of system with no third source to decide.

new_statements.quote: The smallest readily identifiable prosodic unit is the prosodic word, which is the domain of stress assignment. Primary stress in Koasati falls on the first syllable of a word and is associated with the highest F0 and greatest intensity in the word. [...] In addition to intonational tones, Koasati also has tonal accents of three types. First, there is lexical tone associated with certain nouns and certain verbal affixes. Second, tone is used morphologically to convey aspectual distinctions in verbs. Finally, predictable accents may dock on the penultimate syllable of the stem and on heavy syllables (those containing a long vowel or a coda sonorant).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Koasati has an empty rule (qs-tier-2026-09-12) and existing_statements is empty, so this is the first explicit placement: initial primary stress, with a tonal/pitch accent overlay (lexical tone, aspectual tone, penult-of-stem and heavy-syllable pitch accents).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress on the first syllable of the word (highest F0, greatest intensity); on top of this, lexical tone on some nouns and affixes, morphological (aspectual 'grade') tone, and predictable pitch accents that dock on the penultimate syllable of the stem and on heavy syllables (long vowel or coda sonorant); Accentual Phrases carry initial and final H tones.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as secondary stress; §3.3.2: 'The penultimate syllable of the verb root is a recurring docking site for these phonological pitch accents.. may be regarded as a position of metrical prominence, at least diachronically [1, 5] and plausibly synchronically as well.' Heavy syllables also attract predictable accents.
new_statements.exceptions: The initial prominence is realized by pitch and intensity but the initial H of the Accentual Phrase 'may be superseded by a lexical or morphological tone'. Description is of the Louisiana variety.
new_statements.identity_note: Gordon, Martin & Langley 2015 describe 'the variety of Koasati spoken by speakers from Louisiana' (Coushatta, ca. 250 of 300 speakers); Gordon & Martin 2023 draw on the same data. Kimball 1991 (unread here) is based on the Louisiana (Elton) community as well; no Texas-variety statement was found.

new_statements.quote: In Koasati, the first syllable is characteristically the most prominent one (Gordon et al. 2015a), where the prominence is associated most saliently with higher fundamental frequency and increased intensity. The prominence on the first syllable, however, is variable in its realization depending on context and speaker. The higher pitch on the first syllable may be superseded by a phrase-final rise or by a pitch peak on a word that precedes it within a close syntactic constituent [p. 282] ... the intensity is still greatest on the first syllable suggesting that it retains some prominence, plausibly due to word stress. There is no phonetic evidence for rhythmic prominence in Koasati. However, heavy syllables (CVC and CVV) also are prominent [p. 283]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with index 1 (initial word-level prominence, plausibly word stress) and adds: no rhythmic structure, heavy-syllable prominence, phrasal (not word) status of final prominence, and the heavy tonal overlay; also reports secondhand that Kimball 1991 describes default final prominence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: First syllable characteristically most prominent (higher F0, intensity), variably realized and superseded by phrase-final rise or a preceding pitch peak; no rhythmic (iambic) metrical structure; heavy syllables (CVC, CVV) prominent; final prominence is likely phrasal; dense lexical/morphological tone with floating H tones puts Koasati at the tonal end of the Muskogean spectrum.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None as such: 'There is no phonetic evidence for rhythmic prominence in Koasati' (p. 283); heavy syllables prominent; penultimate syllable of the stem is the docking site of aspectual (grade) tone and lexical noun tone (§9.4.2, pp. 284-286, e.g. hopǒːni 'a cook').
new_statements.exceptions: p. 283: 'the final prominence variably observed on final syllables in Koasati is likely a phrasal property'; p. 288: 'The high density of tones coupled with their ability to float situates the Koasati prominence system closest to the tonal end of the spectrum of prosodic systems in Muskogean.' p. 302: Kimball 1991 is cited as describing final syllables of prosodic domains as prominent in the default case.
new_statements.identity_note: Gordon, Martin & Langley 2015 describe 'the variety of Koasati spoken by speakers from Louisiana' (Coushatta, ca. 250 of 300 speakers); Gordon & Martin 2023 draw on the same data. tone_statements.quote: Certain nouns in Koasati are lexically marked for tone whereas, in most nouns, the first syllable is impressionistically most prominent (Gordon et al. 2015). ... Results indicate that the lexical tone is a LH bitonal sequence, which phonetically varies in its timing and scaling as a function of multiple factors including syllable type, following consonant, and speaker. The default prominence on the first syllable is associated with increased intensity and higher F0 (but not greater duration) and may be interpreted as either word-level stress or a phrase-level intonation effect.

tone_statements.quote: Koasati is prosodically complex, featuring lexically marked pitch accents in nouns and verbs, as well as phonologically predictable pitch accents and boundary tones assigned by the intonational system. While most nouns are characteristically associated with a final F0 rise attributed to a phrase-level tone, some have an additional lexically marked high pitch accent on a non-final syllable. The pitch accent system in verbs is more intricate and consists of different types of aspectually determined accents (termed ‘grades’ in the Muskogeanist literature) ...

readall_conflicts: The only listed open copy (Kimball 1991 via archive.org) is a 2-page text excerpt (pp. 609-610) without the accent section, so Kimball's own statement (pp. 26-28) remains unread. Gordon & Martin 2023: 302 report that Kimball 1991 describes final syllables of prosodic domains as prominent in the default case, whereas Gordon, Martin & Langley 2015 state 'Primary stress in Koasati falls on the first syllable of a word' and Gordon & Martin 2023: 282-283 say the first syllable is characteristically most prominent while 'the final prominence variably observed on final syllables in Koasati is likely a phrasal property'. So a Kimball-final vs Gordon-initial disagreement exists at the level of description, which Gordon & Martin resolve by assigning the final prominence to the phrase and the initial prominence to the word; the sources further agree that Koasati has a dense lexical and morphological tone system (aspectual grades, noun tone, floating suffix H tones, penult-of-stem docking) that overlays any word stress.

audit.recode_to: Resolve 'descriptions disagree' in favour of the Gordon/Martin analysis: word-level primary stress fixed on the FIRST syllable (location quantity-insensitive; cues F0 peak + intensity), heavy syllables (CVV, CVC) additionally prominent, no rhythmic/iambic footing; lexical and grammatical (grade) tone on the stem penult; Kimball's noun 'penult-if-long-else-ultima' accent = phrase-final AP/IP intonation per GML 2015 ICPhS sec. 3.1-3.3 and Gordon & Martin 2023: 282-283, 302. Keep Kimball 1991/1994 as the recorded dissent and keep the G&M hedge ('variable in its realization', 'plausibly due to word stress') in the caution field; what counts as heavy CVV+CVC stands.
